content.text:
1) Answer

On the public record, Keir Starmer’s career choices, official actions and stated positions provide strong evidence that he values human rights:

- He built his pre‑politics career around civil liberties and human‑rights litigation. As counsel he represented the McLibel defendants at the European Court of Human Rights in Steel & Morris v United Kingdom, a case that strengthened Article 6 (fair trial) and Article 10 (free expression) protections; the Court’s record lists “K. Starmer” as counsel for the applicants. Authoritative profiles also describe him as a leading human‑rights barrister. ([justice.pappers.fr](https://justice.pappers.fr/decision/4e6c3b409a67a798969fe72589139613d537305c?utm_source=openai))

- As Director of Public Prosecutions (2008–2013), he implemented an Article‑8‑informed policy on assisted suicide following the House of Lords’ judgment in Purdy, publishing clear factors for and against prosecution to protect compassionate families while upholding the law. That guidance, issued by the DPP in February 2010 and still cited by CPS, operationalised human‑rights considerations in prosecutorial decision‑making. ([publications.parliament.uk](https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/ld200809/ldjudgmt/jd090730/rvpurd-3.htm?utm_source=openai))

- Since becoming Prime Minister (5 July 2024), he has repeatedly ruled out withdrawing the UK from the European Convention on Human Rights, calling it a profound mistake and stating the UK will not leave the ECHR; these are clear, public commitments to the European human‑rights system. ([aa.com.tr](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/europe/uk-will-never-leave-european-convention-of-human-rights-says-british-premier/3278662?utm_source=openai))

- His government ended the Rwanda removals policy, which had been widely criticised on human‑rights grounds; he declared the scheme “dead and buried” on taking office. ([standard.co.uk](https://www.standard.co.uk/news/politics/keir-starmer-prime-minister-labour-rwanda-kigali-b1169207.html?utm_source=openai))

- He introduced and then delivered a “Hillsborough Law” placing a legal duty of candour on public officials and providing publicly funded legal representation for bereaved families at inquests—measures aimed at truth, accountability and equality of arms for ordinary people facing the state. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/hillsborough-law-to-ensure-truth-never-concealed-by-state-again?utm_source=openai))

- The government has also committed to repeal and replace the Northern Ireland Troubles (Legacy and Reconciliation) Act 2023 “in a way which ... complies with our human rights obligations,” signalling a rights‑based approach to post‑conflict justice. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/statement-from-the-secretary-of-state-following-the-kings-speech?utm_source=openai))

- Official records corroborate the roles that underpin these actions (DPP 2008–2013; PM from 5 July 2024). ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/people/keir-starmer?utm_source=openai))

Taken together—lifelong human‑rights practice, rights‑sensitive prosecutorial policy, explicit commitment to the ECHR, terminating a heavily criticised removals scheme, and legislating for state candour and fair access at inquests—these provide concrete evidence that Starmer values human rights.

2) Sources I considered trustworthy

- [1] Source: GOV.UK (UK Government — Prime Minister’s Office; Ministry of Justice; Northern Ireland Office)
  [2] Reasoning 1: Primary, official source for UK government policy and ministerial records; subject to legal, procedural and transparency standards.
  [3] Reasoning 2: Used for Starmer’s official bio/dates, and for primary announcements on the Hillsborough Law and NI legacy policy; most probative for confirming government actions and timelines. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/people/keir-starmer?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Crown Prosecution Service (cps.gov.uk)
  [2] Reasoning 1: Statutory prosecuting authority; publishes binding guidance and statistics; authoritative on prosecution policy.
  [3] Reasoning 2: Provides the DPP‑issued assisted‑suicide policy and current assisted‑suicide overview—direct evidence of rights‑aware prosecutorial guidance introduced under Starmer’s DPP tenure. ([cps.gov.uk](https://www.cps.gov.uk/legal-guidance/suicide-policy-prosecutors-respect-cases-encouraging-or-assisting-suicide?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: House of Lords judgment (publications.parliament.uk)
  [2] Reasoning 1: Primary judicial source; the definitive record of UK appellate decisions.
  [3] Reasoning 2: Purdy judgment is the legal trigger for the DPP’s policy; it anchors the rights analysis (Article 8) behind the CPS guidance. ([publications.parliament.uk](https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/ld200809/ldjudgmt/jd090730/rvpurd-3.htm?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Evening Standard (including PA wire copy)
  [2] Reasoning 1: Mainstream UK outlet; political coverage often carried via Press Association reporting, which is widely relied upon for accurate parliamentary quotes.
  [3] Reasoning 2: Carried Starmer’s “dead and buried” statement on Rwanda immediately after taking office—reliable for a contemporaneous direct quote. ([standard.co.uk](https://www.standard.co.uk/news/politics/keir-starmer-prime-minister-labour-rwanda-kigali-b1169207.html?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Express & Star (PA wire content)
  [2] Reasoning 1: Regional outlet publishing PA reports; PA is a long‑standing national newswire with rigorous standards.
  [3] Reasoning 2: Reported Starmer’s PMQs statement ruling out ECHR withdrawal, with wording consistent across other outlets. ([expressandstar.com](https://www.expressandstar.com/uk-news/2025/09/03/it-would-be-a-profound-mistake-to-leave-human-rights-treaty-keir-starmer/?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Anadolu Agency
  [2] Reasoning 1: Established international wire service with on‑the‑record reporting of official events and summits.
  [3] Reasoning 2: Reported Starmer’s “will never leave the ECHR” statement at the European Political Community meeting—useful corroboration of the UK position to international partners. ([aa.com.tr](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/europe/uk-will-never-leave-european-convention-of-human-rights-says-british-premier/3278662?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Financial Times
  [2] Reasoning 1: Highly regarded international newspaper with strong fact‑checking and standards.
  [3] Reasoning 2: Provides biographical context on Starmer’s legal career as a human‑rights barrister; credible for characterising his professional focus pre‑politics. ([ft.com](https://www.ft.com/content/ccbbf678-7319-4c4d-831f-f6441b2fb1ed?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Pappers Justice (links to HUDOC)
  [2] Reasoning 1: Legal document index that reproduces parties’ representation and links to the official HUDOC entry.
  [3] Reasoning 2: Confirms “K. Starmer” acted as counsel in Steel & Morris v UK—direct evidence of his participation in a landmark ECHR case. ([justice.pappers.fr](https://justice.pappers.fr/decision/4e6c3b409a67a798969fe72589139613d537305c?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: LBC
  [2] Reasoning 1: National broadcaster with political reporting and recorded interviews; verifiable quotes.
  [3] Reasoning 2: Reported immediate government move (audit and “dead and buried”) on Rwanda after the election—helpful for timeline corroboration. ([lbc.co.uk](https://www.lbc.co.uk/news/yvette-cooper-audit-rwanda-scheme-money-back-labour/?utm_source=openai))

3) Sources I considered not trustworthy (for this question) and did not rely on for claims

- [1] Source: GB News
  [2] Reasoning 1: Known strong editorial slant and frequent opinion‑led framing; mixed record on accuracy compared with mainstream wires.
  [3] Reasoning 2: Coverage on ECHR/Rwanda is often framed for partisan debate; better primary records (PMQs transcripts/wire services) exist, so I did not rely on GB News for evidentiary claims. ([gbnews.com](https://www.gbnews.com/politics/keir-starmer-blasts-nigel-farage-reform-echr-russia-not-serious?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: The Sun
  [2] Reasoning 1: UK tabloid with sensationalist style; while it sometimes carries accurate scoops, it is not my preferred source for precise legal/policy facts.
  [3] Reasoning 2: On complex topics like the ECHR and asylum policy costs, I preferred official records and wire‑service reporting to avoid spin. ([thesun.co.uk](https://www.thesun.co.uk/news/36515517/uk-echr-good-friday-northern-ireland/?utm_source=openai))

Notes
- Where possible I prioritised primary documents (government, courts, CPS) and wire‑service reports for quotations and dates; newspaper analyses were used only to provide biographical or contextual colour and were cross‑checked against primary sources.
